newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian shares end mixed, BUX index steady.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian shares end mixed, BUX index steady.

text.p: The Hungarian share market inched up to a fifth successive record close on Thursday but the overall picture of the bourse suggested that a phase of calmer trading was imminent, traders said.
The BUX index finished at a fifth successive record closing high of 6,258.25 points, up a marginal 1.20 points.
"Wednesday's intraday correction continued on Thursday in early trading," said Tamas Revesz of Wintrust. "But later prices recovered on revived demand."
Revesz said foreigners remained interested in the market but were becoming increasingly cautious as the market approached the June 16 expiry of BUX futures.
"They are aware of the fact that arbitrageurs will unload their papers on the market," he said, adding the market was witnessing a dumping of shares in the BUX basket.
"This (dumping) will run out after a while, I doubt that anyone will have any positions by June 16," Revesz said.
June BUX futures recovered some of Wednesday's losses and advanced to 6,242.5 points in the last deal from Wednesday's settlement price of 6,200.
On Thursday meat processor Pick Szeged remained a strong gainer as it powered ahead to a new record high of 14,300 forints before retreating to end at 14,000, up 500.
"Foreign demand is very strong for Pick, obviously because of fundamental reasons," Revesz said.
Machinery company Mezogep also surged to a new high of 2,715 forints, before edging lower to close at 2,700 forints, up 220.
The most actively traded MOL gave up five forints to end at 3,545 after a hectic start.
"Some panicking investors beat MOL's price down at the beginning of the session but later it recovered by five-forint steps," Revesz said.

The Budapest Stock Exchange hit five successive closing highs with the BUX index gaining more than five percent in the first three of the sessions. This was followed by hectic trading on Wednesday and a calmer session on Thursday and analysts predict more quiet days to come as the summer holiday season approaches.

"The market is in a danger of drifting sideways, but I think it is going to be a problem not just for Hungary but may be for several markets as well," said Nigel Rendell, emerging market strategist at HSBC James Capel in London.
